title: Prime-to-characteristic specialization invariance for smooth proper morphisms
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ be a smooth proper morphism of schemes [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-weil-proper-morphism], and let $\ell$ be a prime invertible on $S$ (its image is a unit in every local ring). Let $F$ be a locally constant sheaf of $\mathbf F_\ell$-modules on the small etale site $X_{\mathrm{et}}$ of $X$ [def-weil-pbc-etale-site] [def-constructible-locally-constant] [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category], regarded also as an abelian sheaf. For every $q\geq0$, every geometric point $\bar s$ of $S$, and every geometric point $\bar t$ of the strict henselization $S_{(\bar s)}$ [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], the specialization map
$$\operatorname{sp}:(R^qf_*F)_{\bar s}\longrightarrow(R^qf_*F)_{\bar t}$$
is an isomorphism. Higher direct images are those of [def-weil-pbc-direct-image], stalks those of [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks], and specialization is induced by restricting pointed etale neighbourhood germs at $\bar s$ to $\bar t$ through $S_{(\bar s)}\to S$. No relative-dimension or finite-stalk hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0GKD, label lemma-sp-isom-proper-loc-cst-torsion; prime-field specialization and degree-q consequence

proof.text: Let $G$ be the underlying abelian sheaf of $F$. Use the same locally constant datum as $F$: on each localized site the forgetful functor preserves sheafification and therefore sends the constant module sheaf to a constant abelian sheaf. For every module $M$ over $\operatorname{ULift}(\mathbf F_\ell)$, the equality $\ell\cdot1=0$ gives $\ell m=0$. Applied sectionwise this proves that $G$ is torsion. Forgetting scalars commutes with geometric stalks because it preserves filtered colimits, so every stalk element $m$ of $G$ is also killed by $\ell$. Hence $m$ has finite additive order dividing $\ell$. At a geometric point $x$ of $X$, the composite $\mathcal O_{S,f(x)}\to\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\kappa(x)$ sends the assumed unit $\ell$ to a unit. If the residue characteristic is nonzero, the prime $\ell$ therefore does not divide it and is coprime to it. Every divisor of $\ell$, including the order of $m$, is then coprime to the residue characteristic. Characteristic zero is handled separately. No finite-stalk hypothesis is used.

Apply [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-local-acyclicity] to the given smooth morphism $f$. Its conclusion gives universal local acyclicity, hence local acyclicity by taking the identity base change $S\to S$. Only smoothness is used here.

Apply [lem-weil-pbc-locally-constant-torsion-local-acyclicity] to $f$ and $G$. Step 2 supplies local acyclicity, and step 1 supplies local constancy and the prime-to-residue-characteristic torsion condition at every geometric point of $X$. Thus $f$ is locally acyclic relative to $G$, for every geometric point of each strict local base, including geometric points with nonalgebraic field extensions.

Fix $q\ge0$, $\bar s$, and $\bar t$ as in the statement. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-proper-locally-acyclic-specialization] to $f$ and $G$. Properness is an original hypothesis; step 1 gives a torsion sheaf and step 3 gives local acyclicity relative to it. This yields an isomorphism $(R^qf_*G)_{\bar s}\to(R^qf_*G)_{\bar t}$. The cited node specifies the pointed-neighbourhood restriction map, so it is exactly the specialization map claimed here, rather than merely an abstract isomorphism between the two groups. In Lean the statement already forms higher direct images after forgetting scalars to abelian sheaves. The two definitions strictLocalSpecialization and etaleStalkSpecialization are definitionally equal (the differing proofs of the identity-composition condition are proof irrelevant), so the cited theorem applies directly. No derived coefficient comparison is needed.
